column1: Ich gehe {{c1::mit::with (dative)}} meinem Bruder ins Kino.
column2: I am going to the cinema with my brother.
column3: 'mit' always takes the Dative case. (der Bruder -> dem Bruder)

column2: We are driving through the forest.
column3: 'durch' always takes the Accusative case. (der Wald -> den Wald)

column2: The picture is hanging on the wall.
column3: 'an' is a two-way preposition. Here it answers 'where?' (Wo?), so it takes Dative.

column1: Ich hänge das Bild {{c1::an::on (two-way)}} die Wand.
column2: I hang the picture on the wall.
column3: 'an' is a two-way preposition. Here it answers 'where to?' (Wohin?), so it takes Accusative.

column2: We are talking about the weather.
I have been waiting for an hour.
The cat is lying under the table.
column3: 'unter' is a two-way preposition. Here it answers 'where?' (Wo?), so it takes Dative.

column2: The book is lying on the desk.
column3: 'auf' is a two-way preposition. Here it answers 'where?', so it takes Dative.

column1: Er legt das Buch {{c1::auf::onto (two-way)}} den Schreibtisch.
column2: He puts the book onto the desk.
column3: 'auf' is a two-way preposition. Here it answers 'where to?', so it takes Accusative.

column1: Das Auto steht {{c1::vor::in front of (two-way)}} dem Haus.
column2: The car is parked in front of the house.
column3: 'vor' is a two-way preposition. Here it answers 'where?', so it takes Dative.

column2: We are walking around the lake.
